chunks: Indeed, Allah, the Exalted, did not grant people absolute free will in their actions to choose between good and evil; rather, He granted them volition and capacity, and gave them intellect and insight, so that they may know what they choose and recognize what they select.

key_terms.حُرِّيَّةٌ: Absolute free will / Freedom of choice

ai.seo_question: What is the Shia view on free will and predestination?
ai.summary: In *Kamal al-Din*, Shaykh al-Saduq articulates the Shia doctrine of *Amal bayn al-amrayn* (intermediate position), reconciling divine decree with human responsibility by affirming that God created humans with sufficient volition (*iradah*) and capacity (*qudrah*) to choose between good and evil, rather than imposing absolute compulsion (*jabr*) or total freedom (*tafwid*). This nuanced view, championed by the Shia Imams, establishes that while God is the ultimate Creator of all acts, humans are the true agents (*fa'il*) of their choices, thereby justifying divine justice in reward and punishment. The hadith underscores that intellect (*'aql*) and insight (*basirah*) are the divine gifts enabling this informed moral agency.
